# How Rooftop Solar Panels Work

A photovoltaic cell converts sunlight directly into electricity using a
layer of doped silicon. When photons strike the silicon cell, they knock
electrons loose, and the cell's internal structure pushes those electrons in
one direction, producing a direct current. Stacking many cells into a panel,
and many panels into an array, scales this effect up to a useful amount of
power.

Rooftop solar systems need an inverter because a home's appliances and the
electrical grid run on alternating current, not the direct current a
photovoltaic cell produces. The inverter converts the panel's direct current
output into grid-compatible alternating current, and it is usually the
component that determines the system's peak output in kilowatts.

Panel angle and orientation change how much sunlight a rooftop array
collects over a year. A roof facing the equator at an angle close to the
local latitude captures the most annual sunlight, though panels are
sometimes mounted flatter for architectural reasons even if that lowers the
energy the grid-tied system delivers.
